question.text: If the gravitational field in the space is given as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfenced><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mi>K</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></math>. Taking the reference point to be at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> with gravitational potential <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi>kg</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>. Find the gravitational potentials at <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi></math> in SI unit (Given, that <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">J</mi><mo> </mo><mi>cm</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi>kg</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></math>)

solution.text:
Given, E=-Kr2

Gravitational field and gravitational potential is related as E=-dVdr

So, -dVdr=-Kr2

Integrating the above relation,

∫10VdV=∫23Kr2dr

⇒V-10=K12-13

⇒V-10=K6⇒V=66+10⇒V=11 J kg-1
